ta-l1d3q4-d1e97.summary: Transitional paragraph opening the treatment of the parts of the image, first in the first assignment (memory, understanding, will), then in the second. Five questions are posed: what each part is and how they differ; whether they are the soul's essence; whether one arises from another; with respect to which object the image is found in them; and whether the powers are always in act.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e109.summary: First objection that memory does not belong to the image. According to Augustine, what the soul shares with brutes belongs to sensuality, and memory is shared with brutes; the image is not in sensuality.
claims: Memory is common to humans and brutes.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e115.summary: Second objection. Every power that apprehends a determinate difference of time belongs to the sensitive part, not to the intellect, which concerns universals abstracted from time. Memory concerns the past, so it is sensitive.
claims: Apprehension of determinate time belongs to the sensitive part.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e118.summary: Third objection. The Commentator divides intellectual nature into intellect and will, and no philosopher who studied the soul's powers placed memory in the intellective part.
claims: Philosophers divide the intellective part into intellect and will only.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e122.summary: Fourth objection, that understanding (intelligentia) does not belong to the image. Dionysius distinguishes intellectual, rational, sensible, and merely existing beings, and humans fall under the rational, not the intellectual.
claims: Humans are rational rather than intellectual beings in Dionysius's hierarchy.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e125.summary: Fifth objection. Powers are distinguished by acts, but knowing (nosse) and understanding (intelligere) differ only as having a habit and actually contemplating, which belong to the same power. So understanding is not a power distinct from memory.
claims: Having a habit and exercising it belong to the same power.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e128.summary: Sixth objection, that the will does not belong to the image. The will is an operative principle, while the image is to be sought in the highest, speculative part.
claims: The will is operative, while the image is in the speculative part.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e131.summary: Seventh objection from Augustine: the image is in the power of knowing, the likeness in the power of loving. The will is a power of loving, so it belongs to the likeness, not the image.
claims: Augustine assigns image to knowing and likeness to loving.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e137.summary: Eighth objection. What commands and moves others is prior to them, and the will moves all the other powers (Anselm). So it is prior to memory and understanding, and the assignment does not fit the order of persons, since will is appropriated to the Spirit.
claims: The will, moving all other powers, is prior to them.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e140.summary: Thomas's determination. Any property that follows on the soul's essence by its nature is here called a power, whether operative or not. The soul is receptive, since whatever has being from another is possible in itself (Avicenna), and it is not impressed in a bodily organ, since it has an operation independent of the body. So it has the property of retaining what is impressed, and in this sense the soul (or rather the intellect) is the place of species. This retentive power is memory. Because the soul is free from matter and every such nature is intellectual, what it holds it understands, so understanding follows memory. What is understood is grasped as fitting, so the will follows, tending toward the fitting. Nothing further follows, since the will concerns the end and a thing's perfection does not extend beyond its end. Thus memory, understanding, and will are three distinct powers.
claims: Memory in the image is the intellectual soul's retentive property, following its receptivity and immateriality.
Understanding follows memory, and will follows understanding; nothing proceeds beyond the will, which concerns the end.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e144.summary: Reply to the first objection. Memory as taken here is not shared with brutes, since only the intellective soul retains what it receives in itself; the sensitive soul retains in a bodily organ.
claims: Intellectual memory retains in the soul itself; sensitive memory retains in an organ.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e147.summary: Reply to the second objection. 'Memory' is equivocal. As taken here, it abstracts from every difference of time, concerning present, past, and future alike, as Lombard's text says. The memory tied to the past is the sensitive power with its organ at the back of the head, the storehouse of intentions received with but not from sense (Avicenna).
claims: Intellectual memory abstracts from time; sensitive memory concerns the past and has an organ.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e150.summary: Reply to the third objection. The philosophers counted only powers ordered to some act. The soul's retentive property has no act, but in place of an act it simply holds, so they did not mention this memory among the powers.
claims: Intellectual memory has no act beyond retaining, which is why philosophers did not list it.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e153.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. According to Dionysius, the highest of a lower nature touches the lowest of a higher, so the soul at its summit touches the lowest of angelic nature and participates intellectuality. Since the image is assigned to what is best in the soul, it is assigned to understanding rather than reason. Reason is intellectual nature overshadowed, knowing by inquiry and over time what intellect receives at once in full light; hence intellect is said to be of first principles.
claims: The soul at its summit participates angelic intellectuality.
Reason is overshadowed intellect, knowing discursively what intellect sees at once.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e156.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. Knowing (nosse) is holding a thing's knowledge within oneself; understanding (intelligere) is beholding. Every power holds its own habit and object, but only through the power of memory present in it, which follows the essence immediately, since the power of what is prior is always in what is posterior.
claims: Nosse means holding knowledge, intelligere means beholding.
Each power retains only through the power of memory present in it.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e159.summary: Reply to the sixth objection. The will's object is the good, which has the character of end, and there is an end of contemplation as well as of action. So the will relates not only to the active part but also to the contemplative, and belongs to the soul's highest part.
claims: The will relates to the end of contemplation as well as of action and so belongs to the highest part.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e163.summary: Reply to the seventh objection. Augustine uses 'power of knowing' broadly, for what is ordered to knowledge (memory), by which one knows (understanding), and what follows knowledge (will). By 'power of loving' he means the gratuitous habits by which we love God meritoriously. So a sinner who loses God's likeness goes into the region of unlikeness but does not lose the image.
claims: The image lies in the natural powers broadly called cognitive; the likeness lies in gratuitous habits of love.
Sin destroys the likeness but not the image.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e166.summary: Reply to the eighth objection. As in the arts the art concerned with the end commands those concerned with the means (the physician commands the pharmacist), so the will, which regards the end, moves and commands all powers ordered to the end. It is prior in moving but not in being, just as the end is last in being yet moves the efficient cause.
claims: The will is prior in moving but posterior in being, like the end.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e178.summary: First argument that the soul's essence is its powers, from Lombard's text: these three are one mind, one life, one essence.
claims: Lombard says the three powers are one essence.
concepts: una mens una vita una essentia

ta-l1d3q4-d1e184.summary: Second argument. The principle of being and of operating is the same. The soul is the principle of being as the body's substantial form, so it is the principle of operations through itself, without intermediate powers.
claims: The principle of being is also the principle of operation.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e187.summary: Third argument. Substantial form is nobler than accidental form, which operates without an intermediate power. So substantial form does too.
claims: Accidental forms operate without intermediary powers.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e191.summary: Fourth argument. Prime matter is its own passive potency, and form has active potency as matter has passive. So essential form is its own active potency.
claims: Prime matter is its own passive potency.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e194.summary: Fifth argument. Whatever is not of a thing's essence is an accident. Sense and reason, which are powers, are not accidents, since they are principles of substantial differences. So they belong to the soul's essence.
claims: Sense and reason are principles of substantial differences and so not accidents.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e197.summary: Sed contra. Potency relates to essence as being able relates to being, and only in God is being identical with being able. So in nothing else, including the soul, is essence identical with power.
claims: Only in God is esse identical with posse.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e200.summary: Second sed contra. Whatever acts through its essence is a first agent (Avicenna), since every secondary agent acts by participating something added to its essence. The soul is not a first agent, so it acts through powers distinct from its essence.
claims: Only a first agent acts through its essence.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e203.summary: Third sed contra. Perfections are proportioned to what they perfect. The organs of the body differ in the proportion of their mixture, so they are perfected differently by the soul. Not in being, since the soul as substantial form gives one being to the whole body, but in perfections following being, the principles of diverse operations. These are the powers, which must therefore differ from the essence and emanate from it.
claims: The soul gives one being to the whole body but diverse operative perfections to diverse organs.
The powers emanate from the essence and differ from it.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e206.summary: Thomas's determination. A proper and immediate effect must be proportioned to its cause. Where the proximate principle of operation is in the genus of substance, the operation must be substance, and this is true only of God, who alone acts without an intermediary power. In everything else operation is an accident, so its proximate principle must be an accident. The substantial form of fire, for example, acts only through active and passive qualities. The soul likewise acts only through powers, and its powers act perfectly only through habits. The powers flow from the soul's essence, some as perfections of bodily parts operating through the body (sense, imagination), others as existing in the soul itself without need of the body (intellect, will). They are accidents, not common accidents following individual principles, but proper accidents following the species. Yet they belong to the soul's integrity insofar as it is a potential whole made up of diverse powers.
claims: Only in God is operation substance; in every creature the proximate principle of operation is an accident.
The soul's powers are proper accidents flowing from its essence.
The soul is a potential whole whose integrity includes its powers.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e210.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'The three powers are one mind' is not an essential predication but the predication of a potential whole of its parts. 'Mind' is predicated most closely, since these powers belong to the mind as such and constitute the image. 'Life' is less proper, and 'one essence' still less, since the powers are in the essence only as in their origin. A potential whole stands between an integral and a universal whole. A universal is present to each subjective part with its whole being and power and is properly predicated of it. An integral whole is present to no part in being or power and is not predicated of its parts. A potential whole is present to each part with its essence and some power, perfectly only in the highest power, and so is predicated less properly than a universal.
claims: The predication 'three powers are one mind' is that of a potential whole of its parts.
A potential whole stands between integral and universal wholes in how it is predicated of its parts.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e213.summary: Reply to the second argument. The soul's essence is also a principle of operating, but through a power, whereas it is the principle of being immediately, since being is not an accident.
claims: The soul is the immediate principle of being but a mediated principle of operation.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e216.summary: Reply to the third argument. An accidental form is itself the power of another through which an operation is produced, an effect proportioned to it as proximate cause; substantial form is not proportioned to operation in this way.
claims: Accidental form is proportioned to operation in a way substantial form is not.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e219.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. If passive potency means matter's relation or order to form, matter is not its potency, since its essence is not a relation. If potency means a principle in the genus of substance, as act and potency are principles in every genus (Metaphysics 12), then matter is its own potency. Prime matter, the first recipient, relates to passive potency as God, the first agent, relates to active potency: each is its own potency. Intermediate beings have both potencies by participation, and matter's potency is not for operating but only for receiving.
claims: Prime matter is its own passive potency as God is his own active potency.
Intermediate beings have potency by participation.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e222.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. 'Sense' as the name of a power is not the principle of the difference 'sensible'; it is so only as naming sensitive nature, and likewise for the others.
claims: Sense as nature, not as power, grounds the substantial difference 'sensible'.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e234.summary: First objection that one power does not arise from another. Things that exist simultaneously do not arise one from another, and all the powers exist together in the soul from creation.
claims: Simultaneous things do not arise from one another.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e237.summary: Second objection. Every accident is caused by its subject, and one power is not the subject of another, since an accident is not the subject of an accident.
claims: An accident cannot be the subject of an accident.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e240.summary: Sed contra. Powers are determined by acts, and the act of one power naturally follows and originates from another's act, as understanding follows holding knowledge. So too with the powers.
claims: The acts of the powers follow one another in natural order.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e244.summary: Anticipates the reply that the order lies in the acts by reason of the objects rather than the powers. Objects are the perfections and forms of the powers, and perfection is proportioned to what it perfects, so the order returns to the powers.
claims: Objects are perfections of powers, so an order among objects implies an order among powers.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e247.summary: Thomas's determination. Every multitude that descends naturally from one must descend in order, since from one only one proceeds. So the many powers flowing from the soul's essence have a natural order: all flow from the essence, but one through the mediation of another. The later power presupposes the earlier in its definition, and its act depends on the earlier one's act. Understanding, for example, is defined by its act, whose definition includes the phantasm presented by imagination. Similarly, all the accidents of the elements flow from the essence through the primary qualities.
claims: The powers flow from the soul's essence in a natural order, one by mediation of another.
A posterior power includes the prior in its definition.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e250.summary: Reply to the first objection. Although the powers exist together in time, one is naturally prior to another.
claims: The powers are simultaneous in time but ordered by nature.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e253.summary: Reply to the second objection. An accident has no power of itself to produce another accident, but one accident can proceed from substance through another insofar as the first is presupposed in the subject. An accident is not of itself the subject of another, but the subject is subject of one accident through another, as surface is said to be the subject of colour.
claims: One accident can proceed from substance through the mediation of another.
A subject may receive one accident through another, as colour is in surface.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e266.summary: First argument that the image is found in the powers with respect to any object. A power by its nature relates equally to all its objects and is restricted only by habits, and this first assignment is by powers, not habits.
claims: A power of itself relates equally to all its objects.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e269.summary: Second argument from Augustine. We seek the Trinity in the whole of the mind, without separating the action of temporal things from the contemplation of eternal things. All objects are eternal or temporal, so the image concerns any object.
claims: Augustine seeks the Trinity in the whole mind, temporal and eternal.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e275.summary: Contrary argument. The image requires equality, but equality is not found with respect to all objects: I do not will everything as much as I know it.
claims: Equality among the powers is not found with all objects.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e279.summary: Second contrary argument. On this assignment understanding follows memory, but for things known by acquisition, memory follows understanding.
claims: For acquired knowledge, memory follows understanding.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e282.summary: Thomas's determination. An image implies express representation, which in these powers rests on five things. Two, consubstantiality and distinction of powers, are on the side of the soul and hold for any object. Three, equality, order, and actual imitation, concern the objects and vary with them. Equality is of two kinds: of power to power and of power to object. (1) For objects known by acquired habit, the order is not kept, since understanding precedes memory. There is no actual representation of the Trinity, and power-to-power equality holds only in a qualified way, while power-to-object equality does not, since bodies exist more nobly in the soul than in themselves. (2) With the soul as object, the order is kept, since the soul is naturally present to itself and understanding proceeds from knowledge. Power-to-power equality holds simply, since the soul wills and loves itself as much as it understands itself, and power-to-object equality and actual imitation hold too. (3) With God as object, actual imitation is kept, and order most of all, since God is in the soul by essence and is held not by acquisition. Power-to-power equality holds simply, but not power-to-object equality, since God is higher than the soul. So the image is found in some way with any object, more truly with the soul itself, and most truly with God, lacking only power-to-object equality, which matters little to the image.
claims: Express representation in the image depends on consubstantiality, distinction, equality, order, and actual imitation.
The image is found in some way with any object, more truly with the soul as object, and most truly with God as object.
With God as object, every condition is met except equality of power to object, which matters little.
concepts: equality of power to power and to object
God present by essence in the soul

ta-l1d3q4-d1e285.summary: Reply to the first argument. Although the image is assigned to the powers absolutely, it is chiefly found in what is highest in them, namely their relation to objects present in the soul by their essence.
claims: The image is found chiefly in the powers' relation to objects present by essence in the soul.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e288.summary: Reply to the second argument. Augustine holds that there is some image with respect to any object, but especially with respect to God and the soul; he seeks the likeness of the Trinity in many things in order to arrive at the perfect image.
claims: Augustine's search through many trinities aims at the perfect image regarding God and the soul.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e291.summary: The replies to the remaining arguments are evident from what has been said.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e303.summary: First objection that the powers are not always in act regarding the objects of the image. The Philosopher says that when one power is in act, another is withdrawn from its act, and these are three different powers.
claims: When one power is active another is drawn away from its act.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e306.summary: Second objection. The Philosopher says we cannot understand many things at once, and the soul sometimes understands other things, so it does not then understand itself and God.
claims: The intellect cannot understand many things at once.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e309.summary: Third objection. According to Augustine, understanding or seeing requires the knower's intention, which brings the species to the thing. We do not perceive that we always understand the soul and God, so our intellect is not always in act regarding them.
claims: Understanding requires the knower's intention.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e313.summary: Sed contra. The Philosopher says the agent intellect always understands, especially with respect to what is always present to it, such as the soul and God.
claims: The agent intellect always understands.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e316.summary: Second sed contra from Augustine: whatever is in my memory, I remember. The soul and God are always present to memory, so memory is always in act regarding them, and likewise the other powers.
claims: Whatever is in memory is remembered.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e322.summary: Thomas's determination, using Augustine's distinction between thinking (cogitare), discerning (discernere), and understanding (intelligere). Discerning is knowing a thing by its difference from others. Thinking is considering a thing by its parts and properties ('co-agitating'). Understanding is the simple gaze of the intellect on an intelligible present to it. The soul does not always think about or discern God or itself; otherwise everyone would naturally know the whole nature of their soul, which is barely reached with great study. That requires the thing to be present as object and the knower's intention. But in the sense of simple gaze, which is any presence of the intelligible to the intellect, the soul always understands itself and God indeterminately, and an indeterminate love follows. The philosophers give another sense: the soul always understands itself because whatever it understands is illumined by the agent intellect's light and received in the possible intellect. As bodily light is seen in every colour, the agent intellect's light is seen in every intelligible, not as object but as medium of knowing.
claims: The soul does not always think about or discern itself and God, which requires attention and objecthood.
In the sense of simple gaze arising from presence, the soul always understands itself and God indeterminately, with an indeterminate love.
The agent intellect's light is seen in every intelligible as medium, not as object.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e325.summary: Reply to the first objection. The Philosopher's principle applies when powers operate on different objects, when one hinders or withdraws another. When they are ordered to the same object, one helps another, as we more easily imagine what we see.
claims: Powers directed to the same object assist rather than impede one another.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e328.summary: Reply to the second objection. The Philosopher speaks of understanding as the complete operation of an intellect that distinguishes or thinks, not of understanding in the present sense of simple gaze.
claims: The Philosopher's dictum concerns discursive understanding, not simple gaze.

ta-l1d3q4-d1e331.summary: Reply to the third objection. Likewise, the knower's intention is not required for understanding in this sense of simple gaze.
claims: Simple gaze does not require the knower's intention.

ta-l1d3q4-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Question 4 announces the treatment of the parts of the image in the first Augustinian assignment (memory, understanding, will), in five articles: their nature and distinction, relation to the soul's essence, mutual origin, objects, and actuality.

ta-l1d3q4-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 asks what memory, understanding, and will are and how they differ. Against objections that memory is sensitive, temporal, and unknown to the philosophers, that humans are rational rather than intellectual, that nosse and intelligere belong to one power, and that the will is operative, belongs to likeness, and is prior, Thomas derives the three powers in order from the nature of the soul. Its receptivity and immateriality give a retentive intellectual memory, which understands what it holds and wills what it understands as fitting, and nothing goes beyond the will, which concerns the end. The replies distinguish intellectual from sensitive memory, and intellect from reason as overshadowed intellect. They distinguish nosse (holding) from intelligere (beholding) and show that the will concerns the end of contemplation. They locate likeness in gratuitous habits (lost by sin) and image in the natural powers, and they note that the will is prior in moving but not in being.
claims: Memory, understanding, and will are three ordered powers of the intellectual soul.
Intellectual memory abstracts from time and is distinct from sensitive memory.
Sin destroys the likeness, not the image.

ta-l1d3q4-Dd1e170.summary: Article 2 asks whether the soul's essence is its powers. Arguments from Lombard's text, from the soul as principle of being, from accidental form and prime matter, and from sense and reason as substantial principles are met by sed contra arguments. Only in God is esse identical with posse, only a first agent acts by its essence, and diverse organs require diverse operative perfections. Thomas holds that only in God is operation substance. In every creature the proximate principle of operation is an accident, so the soul acts through powers, which are proper accidents flowing from its essence and belonging to it as a potential whole. The replies analyse the potential whole as midway between integral and universal wholes in predication, and they compare prime matter as its own passive potency with God as his own active potency.
claims: The soul's powers are not its essence but proper accidents flowing from it.
Only in God is operation identical with substance.
The soul is a potential whole of its powers.

ta-l1d3q4-Dd1e226.summary: Article 3 asks whether one power arises from another. Against the simultaneity of the powers and the principle that an accident is not the subject of an accident, Thomas holds that, since from one only one proceeds directly, the many powers flow from the essence in a natural order, each through the mediation of a prior one. A posterior power includes the prior in its definition, as understanding includes the phantasm. Simultaneous powers can be naturally ordered, and one accident can inhere through another, as colour is in surface.
claims: The powers flow from the soul's essence in a natural order, one by mediation of another.

ta-l1d3q4-Dd1e258.summary: Article 4 asks with respect to which object the image is found in the powers. Thomas lists five conditions of express representation: consubstantiality and distinction, which hold for any object, and equality, order, and actual imitation, which vary with the object. He examines three cases. For acquired knowledge of external things, order and full equality fail. With the soul as object, all conditions hold. With God as object, everything holds except equality of power to object. So the image is found in some way with any object, more truly regarding the soul, and most truly regarding God.
claims: The image is found most truly in the powers' relation to God, then to the soul itself, and only partially to other objects.
Express representation requires consubstantiality, distinction, equality, order, and actual imitation.

ta-l1d3q4-Dd1e295.summary: Article 5 asks whether the powers are always in act regarding the objects of the image. Thomas distinguishes thinking (cogitare), discerning (discernere), and understanding (intelligere) as simple gaze. The soul does not always think about or discern itself and God, which requires objecthood and intention. But by the presence of the intelligible it always understands itself and God indeterminately, with indeterminate love, and the agent intellect's light is seen in every intelligible as medium. The replies note that powers ordered to the same object assist rather than impede one another, and that the Aristotelian limits apply to discursive, not simple, understanding.
claims: The soul always understands itself and God indeterminately by simple gaze, though it does not always think about them.
The agent intellect's light is seen in every act of understanding as medium.

ta-l1d3q4.summary: Quaestio 4 of Book I, Distinction 3 examines the parts of the first Augustinian image, memory, understanding, and will. Article 1 derives these as three ordered intellectual powers from the soul's receptivity and immateriality. It distinguishes intellectual from sensitive memory and places the image in natural powers and the likeness in gratuitous habits. Article 2 holds that the powers are proper accidents flowing from the essence, since only in God is operation substance, and treats the soul as a potential whole of its powers. Article 3 holds that the powers emanate in a natural order, one through another. Article 4 shows that the five conditions of express representation are met most fully when the powers bear on God, then on the soul itself, and only partially on other objects. Article 5 holds that the soul always understands itself and God indeterminately by simple presence, though it does not always actively think about them.
claims: Memory, understanding, and will are ordered powers flowing as proper accidents from the soul's essence.
The image is found most truly in the powers as directed to God, then to the soul itself.
The soul always understands itself and God indeterminately, though not by active thinking.
